propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review under subsection 72(1) of IRPA regarding a PRRA decision by a Senior Immigration Officer.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review brought under subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA] in relation to a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) decision rendered by a Senior Immigration Officer of the respondent (the Officer).

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application under IRPA subsection 72(1) about a PRRA decision by a Senior Immigration Officer.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed for reasons provided below.
propositions.quote: For the reasons provided below, I have concluded that this application should be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the application for judicial review should be dismissed.

propositions.text: The applicant, Shou Cheng Li, is a Chinese citizen, married with three Canadian-born children.
propositions.quote: The applicant, Shou Cheng Li, is a citizen of the People’s Republic of China (China). He is married with three Canadian-born children.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is a Chinese citizen, married with three Canadian-born children.

propositions.text: Applicant arrived in Canada on Feb 2, 2010, applied for refugee status on Mar 11, 2010, which was refused on Oct 11, 2011.
propositions.quote: The applicant arrived in Canada on February 2, 2010, and submitted a refugee application on March 11, 2010. That application was refused on October 11, 2011.

propositions.text: Applicant sought judicial review of refugee refusal but withdrew after applying for spousal sponsorship for permanent residence.
propositions.quote: The applicant sought judicial review of this refusal but withdrew his application after submitting an application for spousal sponsorship for permanent residence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant arrived in 2010, had a refugee claim refused, sought judicial review but withdrew it after applying for spousal sponsorship.

propositions.text: Spousal sponsorship was refused on Aug 20, 2015 due to misrepresentation by spouse.
propositions.quote: That application was refused on August 20, 2015, as the applicant’s spouse was deemed to have obtained her permanent residence based on a misrepresentation.

propositions.text: Applicant was invited to request a PRRA, which he submitted on Nov 9, 2017.
propositions.quote: Subsequent to this refusal, the applicant was invited to request a PRRA, which was submitted on November 9, 2017.

propositions.text: Applicant’s spouse is appealing the misrepresentation finding.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s spouse is currently pursuing an appeal regarding the misrepresentation finding.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the spousal sponsorship was refused for misrepresentation, applicant submitted PRRA in 2017, spouse is appealing misrepresentation.

propositions.text: Applicant alleges risk of persecution or mistreatment in China for violating the two-child policy (FPP).
propositions.quote: The applicant alleged that, in China, he would be at risk of persecution and/or mistreatment as defined in sections 96 and 97 of IRPA for having violated China’s two-child policy – or Family Planning Policy (FPP).

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges risk of persecution in China for violating the two-child policy.

propositions.text: Officer refused PRRA because applicant’s children are Canadian citizens not facing deportation.
propositions.quote: His children are Canadian citizens and not facing deportation.

propositions.text: Children’s mother is not facing imminent removal, so applicant would arrive in China without family.
propositions.quote: The children’s mother is not facing imminent removal either, so it appears that the applicant would arrive in China without his family.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence that applicant would be perceived by Chinese authorities to have violated FPP.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, there is insufficient evidence that the applicant would be perceived by Chinese authorities to have violated the FPP;

propositions.text: China is more tolerant of children born outside Canada.
propositions.quote: China is more tolerant of children born outside of Canada;

propositions.text: If violation found, applicant would likely face only a fine, not treatment under IRPA sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: Even if Chinese authorities were to conclude that the applicant had violated the FPP, the applicant would likely face only a fine, referred to variously as a “social upbringing charge,” a “social maintenance fee,” or a “social compensation fee.” This penalty applies to all individuals in China and therefore does not amount to treatment of the kind contemplated in sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA;

propositions.text: Applicant may avoid fine if he and wife comply with local/provincial laws for having a third child.
propositions.quote: The applicant may not be fined if he and his wife comply with regulations under China’s local and provincial laws for having a third child.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer refused PRRA, finding insufficient evidence applicant violated FPP, children are Canadian citizens, and any penalty would be a fine only.

propositions.text: Applicant challenges all Officer’s grounds but focuses on insufficiency of evidence that Chinese authorities would perceive FPP violation.
propositions.quote: The applicant takes issue with all of the grounds relied upon by the Officer, but for the purposes of the present case, it is necessary only to deal with the first, concerning the insufficiency of evidence that the applicant would be perceived by Chinese authorities to have violated the FPP.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant challenges all grounds but focuses on the insufficiency of evidence that Chinese authorities would perceive a violation.

propositions.text: Officer found birth permit required before child birth in China.
propositions.quote: From the information before me I ﬁnd that a “birth permit” is required before the birth of a child in China.

propositions.text: Applicant’s children are Canadian citizens not facing removal from Canada.
propositions.quote: I note that the applicant’s children are not facing removal from Canada, as they are Canadian citizens by birth.

propositions.text: Children’s mother has a stayed removal order pending appeal.
propositions.quote: I further note that while the children’s mother was issued a removal order, it is currently stayed, pending an appeal hearing with the Immigration Appeal Division.

propositions.text: Officer unable to conclude wife and children will relocate with applicant to China.
propositions.quote: From the evidence before me I am unable to conclude that the applicant’s wife and children will relocate with the applicant to China.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence to show applicant would be perceived by Chinese authorities to have violated FPP.
propositions.quote: As such, I ﬁnd that there is insufﬁcient evidence before me to demonstrate that the applicant would be perceived by the Chinese authorities to have violated the Family Planning Policy.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found birth permit required, children are Canadian citizens, mother’s removal stayed, and insufficient evidence applicant would be perceived to have violated FPP.

propositions.text: The 2009 evidence about China’s tolerance of children born outside China was additional and not relied on for insufficiency finding.
propositions.quote: From the word “[f]urthermore,” I infer that the 2009 evidence was additional and was not relied on to find an insufficiency of evidence that the applicant would be perceived to have violated the FPP.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the 2009 evidence was additional and not relied on for the insufficiency finding.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Officer presumed he would lie to Chinese authorities about children abroad, which is an error.
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that the Officer’s conclusion quoted above was based on a view that the Chinese authorities would not find out about the applicant’s children abroad because the applicant would not tell them. The applicant argues that the Officer erred in presuming that he would lie to the Chinese authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the Officer erred by presuming he would lie to Chinese authorities about children abroad.

propositions.text: Court disagrees; Officer did not suggest applicant would lie or withhold truth.
propositions.quote: I disagree with the applicant’s premise on this point. There is no suggestion in the Officer’s decision that the applicant would lie or withhold the truth.

propositions.text: Officer concluded insufficient evidence to show Chinese authorities would perceive FPP violation regardless of awareness of children abroad.
propositions.quote: I read the above-quoted passage as a conclusion that, without more evidence, there was not enough to demonstrate that Chinese authorities would perceive a violation of the FPP, regardless of whether they became aware of the existence of the applicant’s Canadian-born children living in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with applicant, finding Officer did not suggest applicant would lie and concluded insufficient evidence regardless of awareness of children abroad.

propositions.text: Applicant submits abundant evidence that having three children violates FPP generally.
propositions.quote: To counter this point, the applicant submits that there is abundant evidence that, generally speaking, having three children is a violation of the FPP.

propositions.text: Applicant submits no evidence except 2009 evidence supports view that situation differs if children do not follow him to China.
propositions.quote: The applicant also submits that there is no evidence, other than the 2009 evidence mentioned above (which was not relied on), to support a view that the applicant’s situation in China would be different if his children did not follow him there.

propositions.text: Officer clearly viewed Chinese authorities as unconcerned about children abroad; court must assess reasonableness of that conclusion.
propositions.quote: Though the Officer did not discuss reasons that Chinese authorities might be unconcerned about the applicant’s children abroad, s/he clearly had that view. Accordingly, I must consider whether the Officer’s conclusion in this regard was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant submits evidence of FPP violation and lack of evidence on children abroad; court must assess Officer’s conclusion reasonableness.

propositions.text: Officer might rely on children’s Canadian citizenship and non-residency to find no burden or cost to China.
propositions.quote: For example, since the children were born in Canada (and are hence Canadian citizens), they would likely not be considered Chinese citizens.

propositions.text: So long as children remain in Canada, they do not burden China; sanctions unlikely for non-citizen, non-resident children.
propositions.quote: More importantly, so long as the children remain in Canada, they do not represent a burden or a cost to China. It would be surprising if sanctions for violating the FPP would be applied in relation to non-citizen, non-resident children.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for Officer to expect applicant to prove he would be perceived to have violated FPP and face sanctions.
propositions.quote: In my view, it was entirely reasonable for the Officer to expect the applicant to bear the burden of proving his assertion that he would be perceived to have violated the FPP and would be subject to sanctions as a result.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it reasonable for Officer to expect proof applicant would be perceived to violate FPP, given children’s citizenship and residency.

propositions.text: Officer did not err in finding insufficient evidence of perceived FPP violation by Chinese authorities.
propositions.quote: Since the Officer did not err in concluding that the evidence was insufficient to find that the applicant would be perceived by Chinese authorities to have violated the FPP,

propositions.text: No need to address alternative issues about sanctions or procedural fairness regarding 2009 evidence.
propositions.quote: it follows that it is not necessary to address alternative issues based on the applicant being subject to sanction. Moreover, since the Officer, in reaching this conclusion, did not rely on the 2009 evidence stating that China is more tolerant of children born outside China, it is also not necessary to address the applicant’s argument that reference to that 2009 evidence represented a denial of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error in Officer’s insufficiency finding and declines to address alternative issues or procedural fairness claims.

propositions.text: Applicant notes wife’s precarious status may force her and children to relocate to China, changing burden situation.
propositions.quote: The applicant notes that his wife’s status in Canada is precarious. She may be forced to leave Canada for China at some point. If so, the applicant’s children may have to follow, since both of their parents would be there.

propositions.text: Officer noted inability to conclude wife and children will relocate with applicant to China.
propositions.quote: The Officer took note of this situation, but was “unable to conclude that the applicant’s wife and children will relocate with the applicant to China.”

propositions.text: Applicant’s concern about children relocating is hypothetical and can be addressed in future PRRA applications.
propositions.quote: In my view, the applicant’s concern that his children will eventually have to go to China must be considered merely hypothetical. This concern could be addressed later, if necessary, in the context of a separate PRRA application by the applicant’s wife and/or children.

propositions.text: Officer’s analysis on this issue was reasonable.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the Officer’s analysis on this issue was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues wife’s precarious status may force relocation; court finds concern hypothetical and Officer’s analysis reasonable.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed for the reasons stated.
propositions.quote: For the foregoing reasons, the present application will be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review for stated reasons.

propositions.text: Parties agreed no serious question of general importance to certify.
propositions.quote: At the hearing, the parties agreed that there is no serious question of general importance to certify.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted a question for certification about fines or fees stopping removal.
propositions.quote: Subsequently, the applicant submitted a question for certification. However, that question concerned whether any fine or fee that might be imposed by Chinese authorities would justify stopping the applicant’s removal.

propositions.text: Court finds proposed question not determinative and declines certification.
propositions.quote: Since I have found that the Officer reasonably concluded that the evidence does not indicate that the applicant will be subject to any such fine or fee, I find that the proposed question is not determinative in this case, and therefore should not be certified.

propositions.text: Judgment: application dismissed; no question of general importance to certify.
propositions.quote: JUDGMENT in IMM-3140-18 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The present application is dismissed. There is no question of general importance to certify.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes parties’ agreement on no question to certify; applicant’s question is not determinative; court dismisses application and denies certification.
